issues.legal_issue: A Hindu male, his wife, and his unmarried daughter can constitute a Hindu undivided family for income-tax purposes despite the absence of an antecedent history of jointness.
material_facts: The assessee's family consisted of himself, his wife, and an unmarried daughter, with no son.
The Department argued that the absence of an earlier joint family or of more than one male prevented the family from being a Hindu undivided family.
issues.conclusion: The assessee, his wife, and his unmarried daughter constituted a Hindu undivided family; neither a prior history of jointness nor a second male member was necessary.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(9), 3, and 55 of the Income-tax Act, 1922 treat a Hindu undivided family, rather than a coparcenary, as a taxable unit. The undefined statutory expression is understood according to Hindu law. A joint Hindu family may include a single male, his wife, and his unmarried daughter; the presumption is that a Hindu family is joint unless division is proved. The Court relied on Gowli Buddanna v. Commissioner of Income-tax and N. V. Narendranath v. Commissioner of Wealth-tax.

predicates.income_tax_assessment: The proceeding concerns the classification of income for income-tax assessment.
predicates.single_hindu_male_with_wife_and_unmarrie: A Hindu male's family consists of him, his wife, and his unmarried daughter, without another male member.
predicates.no_antecedent_jointness: The family has no established history of jointness before the relevant dispute.

issues.definition: When an income-tax assessment concerns a Hindu male whose family consists of him, his wife, and his unmarried daughter, the absence of an earlier history of jointness does not prevent the family from being treated as a taxable Hindu undivided family.

issues.legal_issue: A contention that a transfer into a family's common stock was ineffective because the stock was empty cannot be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court when it was outside the referred question and was not pressed in the High Court.
material_facts: The Department argued before the Supreme Court that the family hotchpot had been empty and that the property therefore could not be blended into it.
The contention had not been raised before the Tribunal, did not arise from the question referred to the High Court, and, although raised there, was not pressed.
issues.conclusion: The Department could not raise that contention before the Supreme Court.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal arising from a reference under section 66(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, the Court would not entertain a contention that was not raised before the Tribunal, did not arise from the reference, and was not pressed in the High Court.

rule.if: tax_reference_appeal and contention_not_raised_before_tribunal and contention_outside_referred_question and contention_not_pressed_in_high_court

predicates.tax_reference_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court arising from a question referred by a tax tribunal to a High Court.
predicates.contention_not_raised_before_tribunal: A party did not raise the contention before the tribunal that made the reference.
predicates.contention_outside_referred_question: The contention does not arise from the question referred to the High Court.
predicates.contention_not_pressed_in_high_court: A party raised the contention in the High Court but did not press it there.

issues.definition: In an appeal arising from a tax reference, a contention is not entertained when it was not raised before the tribunal, falls outside the referred question, and was not pressed in the High Court.

issues.legal_issue: Income from separately owned property first placed in a family hotchpot remains the income of the individual who placed it there when the family consists only of him, his wife, and his unmarried daughter, and no son has acquired an interest by birth.
material_facts: The property was the assessee's self-acquired property and was not an asset of a pre-existing joint family.
The Tribunal accepted as genuine the assessee's declaration that he had placed the property in the family hotchpot.
The family consisted of the assessee, his wife, and his unmarried daughter, and he had no son.
The wife and daughter had rights of maintenance but no right by birth in the property, no right to demand partition, and no right to restrain the assessee from alienating it.
issues.conclusion: The rental income was assessable as the assessee's individual income, not as the income of the Hindu undivided family.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(9), 3, and 55 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, the applicable Hindu-law characterization determines whether income is that of an individual or a Hindu undivided family. For property that did not belong to a subsisting undivided family and acquired a joint-family character for the first time through a declaration, the composition of the family matters. Applying Kalyanji Vithaldas v. Commissioner of Income-tax, the Court held that where no son has an interest by birth, the individual remains owner and the income remains his. It distinguished property already belonging to a subsisting undivided family, which does not lose that character merely because only one coparcener remains, as illustrated by Gowli Buddanna, N. V. Narendranath, and Attorney General of Ceylon v. A. R. Arunachalam Chettiar; it also discussed Commissioner of Income-tax v. Gomedalli Lakshminarayan.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment and property_not_from_subsisting_joint_family and individual_put_separate_property_into_family_stock and family_has_no_son_with_birth_interest

predicates.income_tax_assessment: The proceeding concerns the classification of property income for income-tax assessment.
predicates.property_not_from_subsisting_joint_famil: The property did not belong to a joint family that existed before the individual acquired or contributed it.
predicates.individual_put_separate_property_into_fa: An individual placed property that had been separately his into the family stock.
predicates.family_has_no_son_with_birth_interest: The individual's family has no son who acquired an interest in the property by birth.

issues.definition: When separately owned property is first placed in a family's common stock and no son has an interest in it by birth, the income is assessed as the individual contributor's income rather than as family income.
